client: I've been really struggling since I started this new job at the marketing agency about six weeks ago. Everyone else on my team seems to know exactly what they're doing, and I'm the only one without any real prior experience in marketing, so I constantly feel like I'm falling behind. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I had to try something because the stress is getting pretty unbearable.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out even when you're not sure it will help, and I'm really glad you did. What you're describing — feeling like everyone else has it together while you're the only one struggling — is such a common and painful experience, especially when you're new to a field and still finding your footing. I'm curious: when you look at your colleagues and feel like they "know exactly what they're doing," what specific things are you noticing that lead you to that conclusion?

client: Honestly, it's little things — like when someone asks a question in a meeting and my colleagues just answer confidently without hesitating, or they seem to already know the technical terms and processes without having to look anything up. I sit there and I have to think really hard before I say anything, and half the time I just stay quiet because I'm scared of saying something wrong. It makes me feel like there's some manual everyone else got that I somehow missed.
therapist: That image of a "missing manual" really captures how isolated and behind you feel, and it makes complete sense that you'd feel that way in those moments. Here's something worth gently exploring though — your colleagues have likely been in this field for months or years, so their confidence in meetings may reflect experience rather than some innate ability you lack, and it's possible they had their own "missing manual" feeling when they were six weeks in. When you imagine a brand new colleague joining your team tomorrow with no marketing experience, would you expect them to already know all the technical terms and answer questions without hesitation?

client: I mean... no, I wouldn't expect a brand new person to know everything right away, that's fair. But it still feels different when it's me sitting in that meeting, because everyone already knows I've been there six weeks and I feel like they're watching and judging whether I'm keeping up. It's like I can logically see what you're saying, but in the moment my brain just goes straight to "you should know this by now."
therapist: You've just identified something really important — there's a gap between what you *know* logically and what your brain automatically tells you in the moment, and that automatic thought "you should know this by now" is worth paying closer attention to. That kind of thought often feels like a fact, but it's worth asking: where did that "six weeks = should know everything" rule actually come from, and is there any real evidence your colleagues are actually watching and judging you, or might that be your anxious mind filling in the blanks? What do you think would happen if you did speak up in a meeting and got something slightly wrong?

client: Honestly, that question about where the "six weeks = should know everything" rule came from kind of stopped me in my tracks, because I don't actually know where it comes from. It just feels like this unspoken standard I absorbed somewhere, maybe from watching other people seem so confident so quickly, or maybe just from always putting pressure on myself to be ahead. But if I imagine actually getting something wrong in a meeting, my stomach drops, because I picture everyone exchanging glances like "why did they even hire her," and even if that's my anxious brain filling in blanks, it feels completely real in the moment.
therapist: That gut-drop feeling is so real and valid, even as you're already showing real insight by recognizing it might be your anxious mind writing a story about those exchanged glances rather than what's actually happening. It's worth noticing that you've carried this pressure to "be ahead" for a long time — this job may have just given that old pattern a new stage to play out on. I'm wondering: in your six weeks there, has there been even one small moment where you contributed something, learned something, or got something right that you might be overlooking when your brain jumps straight to the worst-case picture?

client: I mean... yeah, last week my manager did ask me to explain a process to a new hire, which I guess means she trusted me to know it well enough to teach it. But honestly, my brain immediately went to "she probably just couldn't be bothered to do it herself" rather than taking it as a compliment. It's like even when something good happens, I find a way to make it not count.
therapist: What you just noticed about yourself — that even positive evidence gets reinterpreted to keep the negative story intact — is actually a really significant insight, and it's a pattern CBT calls "discounting the positives." Your manager had options; she chose *you* to teach that new hire, and that's a data point worth sitting with rather than explaining away. What do you think it would feel like, even just as an experiment, to let that moment count as genuine evidence that you *do* belong there?

client: Honestly, when you put it that way, I can feel something shift a little — like, okay, maybe that does mean something. But then almost immediately there's this other voice that jumps in and says "she probably just didn't have anyone else available," and I can't tell if that's realistic thinking or if that's exactly the pattern you're describing. It's uncomfortable to sit with the idea that I might actually belong there, because if I let myself believe that and then something goes wrong, I think it would hurt so much more than if I'd just kept my expectations low.
therapist: You've just uncovered something really important underneath all of this — it's not just about doubting your competence, it's that keeping your expectations low feels like *protection* from getting hurt, which makes complete sense as a strategy even though it comes at a real cost. That voice finding alternative explanations isn't realistic thinking, it's your mind working hard to keep you safe from disappointment — but it's also keeping you from fully experiencing the moments where you're actually doing well. I'm curious: has protecting yourself with low expectations actually prevented the pain in the past, or has it just meant you carried the anxiety either way?

client: That question actually hit harder than I expected, because when I really think about it... no, it hasn't actually stopped the pain. I still felt awful when things went wrong at work, maybe even worse because I'd spent so much energy bracing for it beforehand. So I've basically been anxious the whole time AND still got hurt when it happened, which feels kind of pointless when you say it out loud like that.
therapist: You just made a really powerful connection on your own — that the "protection" strategy has actually been costing you twice, once in all the anticipatory anxiety and again when difficult moments still land hard anyway. That kind of honest self-observation is genuinely hard to do, and it's exactly the kind of insight that can start to loosen the grip of these patterns over time. I'm wondering: now that you can see that the low-expectations strategy hasn't been keeping you safe, what might it feel like to experiment — just gently, just a little — with letting some of the good evidence in, like your manager choosing you last week?

client: Honestly, when you put it that way, I can see the logic of it, but letting that good evidence in feels almost dangerous, like I'm setting myself up for a bigger fall if things go wrong later. When my manager chose me last week, my first instinct was to think there must have been no one better available, not that I actually deserved it. I guess I'm scared that if I start believing the good stuff, I'll just be more crushed when the bad stuff inevitably happens.
therapist: That word "inevitably" is really worth pausing on — it suggests your mind has already decided that bad things *will* happen, which means you're essentially living under a threat that hasn't occurred yet, and that's an exhausting way to exist. What's interesting is that believing good evidence doesn't actually make you more fragile when hard things happen — in fact, a more balanced view of yourself might give you more resilience to weather those moments, not less. I'm curious: if a close friend came to you and said they were too scared to believe anything good about themselves in case it hurt more later, what would you want them to know?

client: I hear what you're saying, and honestly, if a friend said that to me, I'd probably tell them they deserve to feel good about themselves without always waiting for the other shoe to drop. But it feels different when it's me, like the rules just don't apply the same way. I guess I don't fully trust that I'd actually be more resilient if I let myself believe good things, because what if believing them is exactly what makes the fall harder?
therapist: The fact that you'd so readily offer your friend compassion and permission to feel good, but can't quite extend that same grace to yourself, tells us something important — somewhere along the way you learned that *you* specifically need to be held to a harsher standard, and that's worth exploring gently over time. On your fear that believing good things makes the fall harder — there's actually no evidence that's true, and in fact people who can acknowledge their strengths tend to have more solid ground to stand on when things get tough, not less. I'm wondering: where do you think you first learned that the kinder rules you'd apply to everyone else just didn't apply to you?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. I think... maybe it started with my mom, like she had really high expectations and whenever I did something well she'd immediately point out what could have been better, so I just internalized that voice. I never really thought about it as a "rule" I learned, it just feels like the truth about me, you know?
therapist: What you just shared takes real courage, and it's such an important piece of the puzzle — that relentless inner critic isn't actually *the truth about you*, it's your mother's voice that you've carried so long it started to feel like your own. It makes complete sense that a child who was met with "what could be better" instead of "I'm proud of you" would grow up scanning for their own flaws before anyone else could find them, because that felt safer. I'm wondering: when you hear that inner critic telling you that you don't belong at your job or that the good things don't count, can you notice it now as that inherited voice rather than an objective truth about who you are?
